Problem 1¶

Points: 20

In this problem we will use data on infidelity, known as the Fair's Affairs dataset. The Affairs dataset is available as part of the datasets package instatsmodels. This data comes from a survey conducted by Psychology Today in 1969, see Greene (2003) and Fair (1978) for more information.

The dataset contains various self-reported characteristics of 6366 participants, including how often the respondent engaged in extramarital sexual intercourse during the past year, as well as their gender, age, year married, whether they had children, their religiousness (on a 5-point scale, from 1=anti to 5=very), education, occupation (Hillingshead 7-point classification with reverse numbering), and a numeric self-rating of their marriage (from 1=very unhappy to 5=very happy).

(a) Describe the participants. Use descriptive, summarization, and exploratory techniques to describe the participants in the study. Tell us the average/mean of children count ? What is the average age of respondents? In your response comment on any ethical and privacy concerns you have with this dataset.

Out of 6366 people who participated in the study, average age was 29 years in a range of 17 to 42, and who had spent almost 9 years on avg in their current marriages in range of 0 years (newly married) to 58 years.Most participants had some college education and held white-collar related jobs and enjoyed very happy marriages. Despite those people being generally happy in their marriages, they still reported extramarital affairs.More than one-third (= 38%) of particpants were fairly religious in their practices. Each respondent has atleast 1 children (in range of 0 to 5). The person who spent the maximum hours in affairs was highly satisfied in his/her marriage, yet was young and almost married for 2.5 years and had some college level education. 4313 respondents out of 6366 (approx 68%) reported zero extra-marital affairs.2414 participants had no children and has extra-martial relationship hours .¶

Ethical and Privacy concerns:¶

The dataset contains highly sensitive personal information like marriage satisfaction, infidelity, religious beliefs. There is no clear indication if participants agreed to the their data being distributed publicly or researced on a large scale basis which can be a violation. With the given attributes in the dataset, it can be possible to track down individuals in a small town which is against re-identification norms. The data can potentially bring stereotype thinking and hamper moral judgement of certain people initiating bias.

(b) Suppose we want to explore the characteristics of participants who engage in extramarital sexual intercourse (i.e. affairs). Instead of modeling the number of affairs, consider the binary outcome - had an affair versus didn't have an affair. Create a new variable to capture this response variable of interest. What might the advantages and disadvantages of this approach to modeling the data be in this context?

So, 4313 people had no affair so value of yes_affair is 0 for them. Rest had atleast one affair. So variable value is 1 for them. The advantage of having this variable is that it will help to find out the probablity of a person having an affair. This will likely help to understand better why people have affair or just reduce skew and model with logistic regression.The disadvanatge is removes the concept of knowing the number of times a person had affair and almost making the fact that a person having affair once is same as the person having affair multiple times.There can be potential loss of information.¶

A p-value below 0.05 indicates a statistically significant predictor.Here¶

  1. rate_marriage (with coefficient -0.7161) and p<0.001 shows higher marriage satisfaction is associated with lower likelihood of having an affair.This is the most powerful predictor here.
  2. religious (with coefficient -0.3752 ) and p<0.001 means more religious persons are less inclined to having an affair.
  3. age (with coefficient -0.0605) and p<0.001 means old people are less inclined to having affairs than young and mid-aged.
  4. educ (with coefficient -0.0392) and p<0.001 means higher education slightly reduces the likelihood of having an affair.
  5. occupation (with coefficient 0.1602 )and p<0.001 means people in higher occupation levels have less likelihood of affair.
  6. yrs_married (with coefficient 0.1100 )and p<0.001 means people who are longer marraied are slightly more likely to have an affair.
  7. Similarly with occupation (with coefficient 0.1602) means participants in higher occupational categories have a modestly higher likelihood of engaging in affairs. All these above are positive predictors.
  8. Other predictors like children ,occupation_husb have high p-values meaning they do not significantly predict whether someone had an affair:
  9. LLR p-value: 5.807e-224 says the model overall is highly significant and predictors collectively improve prediction of affairs.
  10. Pseudo R-squ.: 0.1327 shows that the model explains about 13% of the variation in affair behavior.

(d) Use a model selection procedure to obtain a "best" fit model. Is the model different from the full model you fit in part (c)? Which variables are included in the "best" fit model? [Hint: stepwise selection]

Model Selection Procedure¶

Reference -- https://www.statology.org/stepwise-selection/¶

reference-- https://uw.hosted.panopto.com/Panopto/Pages/Viewer.aspx?id=9884004c-b749-4923-bdfc-b217000c37e3&start=1270.1¶

---https://medium.com/@kelvinsang97/feature-selection-stepwise-regression-forward-selection-and-backward-elimination-with-python-d53230be995c

We will implement here a Stepwise logistic selection which selects the best subset of predictors using model fit criteria.¶

In [100]:
# reference (OpenAI, 2025)
def stepwise_selection(X, y, 
                       initial_list=[], 
                       threshold_in=0.01, 
                       threshold_out=0.05, 
                       verbose=True):
    
    included = list(initial_list)
    while True:
        changed=False
        
        # forward step
        excluded = list(set(X.columns) - set(included))
        new_pvals = pd.Series(index=excluded, dtype=float)
        for col in excluded:
            model = sm.Logit(y, sm.add_constant(pd.DataFrame(X[included + [col]]))).fit(disp=0)
            new_pvals[col] = model.pvalues[col]
        best_pval = new_pvals.min() if len(new_pvals)>0 else None
        
        if best_pval is not None and best_pval < threshold_in:
            best_feature = new_pvals.idxmin()
            included.append(best_feature)
            changed=True
            if verbose:
                print("Add  {:20} with p-value {:.4f}".format(best_feature, best_pval))
                
        # backward step
        model = sm.Logit(y, sm.add_constant(pd.DataFrame(X[included]))).fit(disp=0)
        pvals = model.pvalues.iloc[1:]
        worst_pval = pvals.max()
        
        if worst_pval > threshold_out:
            worst_feature = pvals.idxmax()
            included.remove(worst_feature)
            changed=True
            if verbose:
                print("Drop {:20} with p-value {:.4f}".format(worst_feature, worst_pval))
        
        if not changed:
            break
            
    return included

The step wise model is different from full model since stepwise best model has only 5 predictors against 8 predictors of full-model.¶

The variables included in best fit model are rate_marriage,yrs_married, religious, age and occupation.Stepwise selection removed three variables from the full model: children, educ, and occupation_husb. Therefore, the best model is smaller and more parsimonious than the full model while still capturing all meaningful predictors of yes_affair.

(e) Interpret the model parameters using the model from part (d).

  • rate_marriage: Effect: Negative Interpretation: As marital satisfaction increases, the likelihood of having an affair decreases sharply.

Odds ratio explanation: If the coefficient was about –0.72 (from the earlier logit model):A one-unit increase in rate_marriage (e.g., going from 3 to 4 on the satisfaction scale) cuts the odds of an affair in half.This is the strongest protective factor in the model.

  • yrs_married :Effect: Positive Interpretation: The longer a person has been married, the more likely they are to have an affair.

Odds ratio: If the coefficient was ~0.11:Each additional year of marriage increases the odds of an affair by 12%.It’s a moderate but meaningful risk factor.

  • religious:Effect: Strong negative Interpretation: More religious individuals are less likely to have an affair.

Odds ratio: If the coefficient was –0.375:For each increase in religiousness (e.g., from "rarely attends" → "often attends"), the odds of cheating decrease by about 31%.Religion is another strong protective factor.

  • age:Effect: Negative Interpretation: Older individuals are less likely to have an affair. Odds ratio: With coefficient around –0.06:Each additional year of age reduces the odds of an affair by about 6%.Age has a small but consistent protective effect.

  • occupation:Effect: Positive Interpretation: Some occupations are associated with a higher likelihood of having an affair.

Odds ratio:If coefficient is ~0.16:Higher occupational categories increase the odds of an affair by 17% per category level.This likely reflects differences in workplace socialization, independence, or opportunity.

plt.xlabel("Marital Satisfaction (1 = Very Unhappy, 5 = Very Happy)")

The predicted probabilities increase exponentially as marital satisfaction goes from 1 to 5 — because the y-axis is on a log scale, and the points lie on a straight line, indicating exponential growth in probabilities.However, these probabilities are extremely small in absolute terms.This is counterintuitive, because the model's theory and coefficients say higher marital satisfaction should decrease the probability of an affair, not increase it.¶

(g) Reflect on your analysis in this problem. After completing all the parts of this analysis what remaining and additional ethical and privacy conerns do you have?

  • Sensitivity and confidentiality: The dataset involves highly personal and potentially stigmatizing information about individuals’ marital fidelity, religion, age, occupation, etc. Misuse or careless handling can lead to harm or discrimination.Even if data is anonymized, certain combinations of features (e.g., occupation + age + years married) might indirectly identify individuals, especially in small subgroups.
  • Informed Consent :It’s critical that participants gave informed consent for their data to be collected and analyzed, especially for sensitive topics.Participants should have been clearly informed about how their data will be used, stored, and who will have access.
  • Data Security and Storage :Sensitive data must be stored securely, encrypted, and access-controlled.
  • Model Transparency and Fairness :It’s essential to communicate clearly that predictions are probabilistic and not deterministic — they can never “prove” who will have an affair. The model may be biased due to sample selection or missing variables; care must be taken to avoid overgeneralization.

Problem 2¶

Points: 20

In this problem set, we will use some data from a sports context. The data is provided as part of the Introduction to Statistial Learning with Applications in Python textbook. It was taken from the StatLib library which is maintained at Carnegie Mellon University. The data provided is part of the data that was used in the 1988 ASA Graphics Section Poster Session. The salary data were originally from Sports Illustrated, April 20, 1987. The 1986 and career statistics were obtained from The 1987 Baseball Encyclopedia Update published by Collier Books, Macmillan Publishing Company, New York.

Following the directions below to load this data, Hitters directly from the ISLP python package. You may need to install the ISLP package before you can get started. In the Jupyter Hub you can open a terminal and use pip install ISLP. Next load the data as follows:

(a) Develop your own question to address in this analysis. Your question should be specific and measurable, and it should be able to be addressed through a basic analysis of the Hitters dataset. Hint: you will need to get to know this dataset and the variables available to formulate an appropriate question.

Question : Do players with more career hits (CHits) tend to earn higher salaries?¶

Reference read--https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/floser/hitters¶

The predictor variable will be CHits (Career Hits) and outcome variable (Salary). Salary tends to be a measure of player's value in a league.CHits means long-term performance of the player. Missing values of Salary needs to be removed for analysis. This is possible to measure it using a scatterplot of CHits Vs. salary

The regression equation Salary = 260.04 + o.382 * CHits¶

Intercept (260.04) means the expected salary for a player with zero career hits. Slope (0.382) means for each career hit, a player's salary increases by about $382( Assuming salary measured in dollars). This indicates a positive relation as in the correlation. The |t| value for CHits is 10.609 and p-value is 0.000 (less than 0.05). This show CHits is a significant predictor of salary and there is strong statiscal evidence that players with more career hits get higher salaries. R-squared is 0.301 meaning about 30% of variation in player salary is impacted by Career hits alone.

(b) Briefly summarize the dataset, describing what data exists and its basic properties. Comment on any issues that need to be resolved before you can proceed with your analysis.

The Hitters dataset contains information on Major League Baseball players, including their performance statistics from the 1986 season, cumulative career performance, and salary data. The dataset includes 322 observations (players) and 20 variables covering batting performance, fielding performance, player experience, league affiliation, and salary.¶

Types of Variables in the Dataset Season performance variables (1986): AtBat, Hits, HmRun, Runs, RBI, Walks These measure how a player performed during the 1986 season.

Career performance variables: CAtBat, CHits, CHmRun, CRuns, CRBI, CWalks These summarize a player’s cumulative career achievements up to 1986.

Experience and position-related variables: Years (years in the MLB), PutOuts, Assists, Errors

Categorical variables: League, Division, NewLeague These indicate the league (American or National) and division.

Salary variable: Salary — player’s 1987 salary in thousands of dollars.

Issues- There are 59 salary values which have no data. Since Salary is primary outcome like in abaove anaylsis, rows with missing salary values must be removed before making analysis.

(c) Use the dataset to provide empirical evidence that addressed your question from (a). Discuss your results. Provide at least two visualizations to support your story.

As done in step a), the evidence to support the answer to the question is Correlation evidence. The correlation between Chits and Salary is r= 0.5489.This indicates a positive moderate relationship. Players with more career hits tend to have higher salaries.¶

The evidence from regression equation Salary = 260.04 + o.382 * CHits says, CHits coefficient is highly statistically significant(p <0.001). For each additional career hit, salary increase by $382. Hence this is strong statistical evidence for player with more career hits earn higher salaries.¶

The question was well-defined in the analysis and it was specific (named the variables), measurable (used quantitative data), and answerable using simple statistical tools.I was able to find the answer through correlation analysis, scatterplot and regression-line visualization, and simple linear regression model.¶

Problem 3¶

Points: 20

In this problem, we will use data available in Machine Learning with R by Brett Lantz. This data was available in the public domain and a few version exist online.

The data describe individual medical costs billed by health insurance. For each observation, there is information about:

  • age: age of primary beneficiary of the insurance policy
  • sex: the person's sex, measured here a binary gender
  • bmi: body mass index, providing an understanding of body, weights that are relatively high or low relative to height, (kg / m ^ 2)
  • children: number of children/dependents covered by health insurance
  • smoker: smoking status of the primary beneficiary
  • region: the beneficiary's residential area in the US, northeast, southeast, southwest, northwest.
  • charges: medical costs billed by health insurance

In our analysis, we will be interested in the relationship between charges and the individual characteristics measured.

(b) Fit a multiple linear regression model. How much variance in the medical costs(charges) does this variable- bmi explain?

Multiple Linear Regression model written as Y = B0 + B1X1 + B2X2 + B3X3 + B4X4 + B5X5 + B6X6 + e¶

where 1,2,..6 are predictors¶

B1, B2, ... B6 are the parameters are estimated using the same least squares approach, using a computer.¶

We interpret Bi as the average effect on Y per one-unit increase in X holding all other predictors fixed where i is the number of predictors.¶

reference --https://canvas.uw.edu/courses/1830727/pages/7-dot-7-multiple-linear-regression?module_item_id=24478640¶

Here the regression equation would be charges = B0 + B1 * age + B2 * bmi + B3children + B4smoker + B5sex + B6region + e

Interpretation of the results above¶

  • age (coef = 256.86): Older people tend to have higher charges.
  • bmi (coef = 339.19): Higher BMI increases charges.
  • children (coef = 475.50): More children slightly increases charges.
  • smoker_yes (coef = 23850): Smoking drastically increases medical costs.
  • region_southeast and region_southwest: Slight negative effect compared to the baseline (region_northeast).

Non-significant predictors:

R-squared = 0.751 --> About 75.1% of the variance in medical charges is explained by all predictors combined (age, bmi, children, sex, smoker, region). This is quite high for a healthcare cost dataset. Significant predictors (p < 0.05):

  • sex_male, region_northwest → Their coefficients are not significantly different from zero.

(c) Evaluate the statistical assumptions in your regression analysis from part (b) by performing a basic analysis of model residuals and any unusual observations. Discuss any concerns you have about your model.

reference -- https://www.statology.org/linear-regression-assumptions/¶

Linearity : The relationship between predictors and the response is linear. Independence : Residuals are independent (no autocorrelation). Homoscedasticity: Constant variance of residuals across all levels of predictors. Normality of residuals: Residuals are approximately normally distributed. No Multicollinearity: Independent variables should not be highly correlated with each other.

In [157]:
import scipy.stats as stats
# Assuming 'model' is fitted OLS model, Extract residuals and fitted values

residuals = model.resid
fitted = model.fittedvalues
In [158]:
# Residuals vs Fitted (Linearity & Homoscedasticity)
plt.figure(figsize=(8,5))
plt.scatter(fitted, residuals, alpha=0.5)
plt.axhline(0, color='red', linestyle='--')
plt.xlabel('Fitted values')
plt.ylabel('Residuals')
plt.title('Residuals vs Fitted values')
plt.show()

The scatterplot shows there is no linear relationship between residuals and the fitted values. If linearity is violated, the model may underestimate or overestimate the

effect of predictors. There is a presence of certain cone shape in the plot of fitted values but is very wide and this can shows presence of somewhat of Homoscedasticity. But Homoscedasticity

can make standard errors unreliable i.e. p-values and confidence intervals may be invalid.

In [162]:
# Normality using Q-Q plot
plt.figure(figsize=(6,6))
stats.probplot(residuals, dist="norm", plot=plt)
plt.title('Q-Q Plot of Residuals')
plt.show()

Here we can see the residuals clearly depart from a straight diagonal line, which indicates that they do not follow normal distribution: This can be because of presence of outliers which

which affect normal distribution. Non-normality affects confidence intervals and hypothesis tests, though coefficients remain unbiased.

(d) Use a stepwise model selection procedure of your choice to obtain a "best" fit model. Is the model different from the full model you fit in part (b)? If yes, how so?

References -- https://canvas.uw.edu/courses/1830727/pages/7-dot-8-variable-selection?module_item_id=24478641¶

https://github.com/talhahascelik/python_stepwiseSelection/blob/master/stepwiseSelection.py

Stepwise regression iteratively adds or removes predictors based on some criterion (usually AIC, BIC, or p-value) to find a model that balances goodness-of-fit and simplicity. Akaike information criterion (AIC) Bayesian information criterion (BIC)

Forward selection: Start with no variables, add the most significant predictor at each step. Backward elimination: Start with all variables, remove the least significant predictor at each step. Both (stepwise): Combines forward and backward selection.

In [164]:
# Forward selection

# Start with y and full candidate predictors
y = df["charges"]
X = df.drop(columns=["charges"])

# reference -- (OpenAI,2025)
def forward_selection(X, y):
    remaining = list(X.columns)
    selected = []
    current_score, best_new_score = np.inf, np.inf
    
    while remaining:
        scores_with_candidates = []
        
        for candidate in remaining:
            formula_vars = selected + [candidate]
            X_train = sm.add_constant(X[formula_vars])
            model = sm.OLS(y, X_train).fit()
            scores_with_candidates.append((model.aic, candidate))
        
        scores_with_candidates.sort()
        best_new_score, best_candidate = scores_with_candidates[0]

        if best_new_score < current_score:
            remaining.remove(best_candidate)
            selected.append(best_candidate)
            current_score = best_new_score
        else:
            break
            
    return selected
    
# Run Forward selection    
selected_features = forward_selection(X, y)
selected_features

The Breast Cancer Wisconsin (Original) dataset contains 699 observations of breast tumor samples collected using fine-needle aspiration (FNA). Each observation represents a tumor and is described by 10 attributes:¶

1 ID field 9 predictive diagnostic features The class field values 2 = benign, 4 = malignant

All nine diagnostic features are integer values from 1 to 10, each measuring a different property of the cell nuclei observed under a microscope. These features include clump thickness, uniformity of cell size/shape, bare nuclei, mitoses, and others.

One attribute, Bare Nuclei, contains some missing values, represented as "?" in the raw data.

The goal of the dataset is to predict whether a tumor is benign or malignant based on these cell characteristics.

Actual: Benign                   125                     2

From the Confusion Matrix¶

 TN(True Negatives) = 125 ---The model correctly identified 125 benign cases.
 FP(False Positives) = 2 --The model predicted malignant, but the tumor was actually benign.This can be followed by testing like biopsy to ascertain.
 FN(False Negatives)= 7 --The model predicted benign, but the tumor was actually malignant. This is  most serious since cancer can go untreated or detected late and is not beneficial for patient.
 TP (True Positives) = 71 --The model correctly identified 71 malignant tumors.

The confusion matrix on the 30% test set shows 125 true negatives and 71 true positives, indicating strong overall predictive performance. The model misclassified 2 benign tumors as malignant (false positives) and 7 malignant tumors as benign (false negatives).In the context of cancer diagnosis, false negatives are the most problematic error, because a malignant tumor mistakenly identified as benign may delay essential treatment and significantly worsen patient outcomes. False positives, while undesirable, lead only to additional testing and do not directly endanger the patient.

Problem 5¶

Points: 10

Please answer the questions below by writing a short response.

(a) Describe three real-life applications in which classification might be useful. Describe the response, as well as the predictors. Is the goal in each application inference or predictions? Explain your answer.

Below are real-life applications in which classification can be useful. 1)Email Spam Detection: Response :Whether an email is spam or not spam Predictors: Frequency of certain keywords, Sender’s address,Email formatting (HTML vs. plain text),Presence of attachments Goal: Prediction --The objective is to automatically classify new incoming emails. We are not primarily interested in why a given email is spam, only that we can correctly identify it.

2)Medical Diagnosis (e.g., diabetes prediction) Response :Whether a patient has diabetes or does not have diabetes. Predictors: Age, BMI, Blood pressure, Glucose levels, Frequency of using loo/day, Frequency in drinking water/day, Family History Goal: Both, but typically inference + prediction --Doctors may want inference (e.g., which factors are significant, how glucose level relates to risk), but machine-learning systems often focus on prediction for early detection. The relative goal depends on context.

3)Credit Card Fraud Detection Response :Fraudulent vs. legitimate transaction. Predictors: Transaction amount, Merchant location, Time of day, Device used, Historical user behavior Goal: Prediction -- The main goal is to flag suspicious transactions in real time. Understanding the causes of fraud is less important than catching fraudulent events accurately.

References -- https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405844018353404 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10107388/ https://www.researchgate.net/publication/369434510_Credit_Card_Fraud_Detection_Using_Predictive_Model

b) Describe three real-life applications in which regression might be useful. Describe the response, as well as the predictors. Is the goal in each application inference or predictions? Explain your answer.

Here are three real-life regression applications, mentioned with the response, predictors, and whether the goal is inference or prediction: 1)Predicting House Prices: Response :The sale price of a house (continuous). Predictors: Square footage, Number of bedrooms/bathrooms, Neighborhood quality, Age of the property , Lot size, Location, School district ranking Goal: Prediction --The model is used to estimate prices for homes not yet sold. The priority is accurate prediction rather than understanding how each feature affects price.

2)Estimating the Effect of Advertising on Sales: Response :Product sales (continuous). Predictors: Advertising expenditure on TV, Advertising on radio, Social media ads, Price promotions Goal: Inference -- A business may want to know which advertising channels significantly increase sales and how much. The emphasis is on understanding relationships, not just forecasting.

3)Predicting a Patient’s Blood Pressure: Response :Systolic blood pressure(continuous). Predictors: Age , Weight or BMI , Sodium intake, Stress level , Physical activity Goal: Both, but typically prediction --Clinicians may use the model to predict blood pressure for new patients, though they may also use coefficients for inference (e.g., understanding how age affects blood pressure). In many practical ML tasks, prediction is the primary aim.

References: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-84394-5_19 https://www.researchgate.net/publication/346092476_Social_Media_Advertisement_and_its_Effect_in_Sales_Prediction_-_An_Analysis https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1746809421004109

(c) What are the advantages and disadvantages of a very flexible (versus a less flexible) approach for regression or classification? Under what circumstances might a more flexible approach be preferred to a less flexible approach? When might a less flexible approach be preferred?

Advantages of a very flexible approach

  1. Can capture complex relationships: Flexible models (e.g., splines, decision trees, neural networks) can fit highly nonlinear patterns between predictors and response.
  2. Lower bias: They can adapt closely to the training data, reducing systematic errors.
  3. Better performance with large, complex datasets: When there is enough data, flexible models often achieve higher predictive accuracy.

Disadvantages of a very flexible approach

  1. Higher variance / overfitting risk: They can fit the noise in the training data, leading to poor generalization.
  2. Harder to interpret: Understanding the effect of individual predictors is difficult.
  3. Computationally expensive: More parameters often mean longer training times and higher resource usage.

Advantages of a less flexible approach

  1. Lower variance / less overfitting: Simple models (e.g., linear regression, logistic regression with few predictors) generalize better on small datasets.
  2. Easier to interpret: Coefficients and relationships are transparent, which is useful for inference.
  3. Faster and simpler: Less computational burden and simpler to implement.

Disadvantages of a less flexible approach

  1. Higher bias: May fail to capture nonlinear relationships, underfitting the data.
  2. Poor performance on complex datasets: Simple models can miss subtle patterns, reducing predictive accuracy.

We can opt for more flexible approach when the relationship between predictors and response is complex or nonlinear or when dealing with very large datasets and focussing on prediction accuracy than interpretability. Less flexible approach is opted usually when the data is limited and giving importance to Simplicity and interpretability such as in regulatory, medical, or financial contexts. Also when the relationshio between predictors and response is linear.

References: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/machine-learning/ml-classification-vs-regression/ https://businessanalyticsinstitute.com/regression-vs-classification-differences/ https://brainly.com/question/32929146

Problem 6¶

Points: 10

Suppose we have a dataset with five predictors, $X_1 =$ GPA, $X_2 =$ IQ, $X_3 =$ Gender (1 for Female, and 0 for Male), $X_4 =$ Interaction between GPA and IQ, and $X_5 =$ Interaction between GPA and Gender. Note: the data here is limited as gender was collected as a binary variable.

The response is starting salary after graduation (in thousands of dollars). Suppose we use least squares to fit the model and get $\hat{\beta}_0=50, \hat{\beta}_1=20, \hat{\beta}_2=0.07, \hat{\beta}_3=35, \hat{\beta}_4=0.01$, and $\hat{\beta}_5=-10$.

(a) Which answer is correct and why? [single choice question]

i. For a fixed value of IQ and GPA, males earn more on average than females.

ii. For a fixed value of IQ and GPA, females earn more on average than males.

iii. For a fixed value of IQ and GPA, males earn more on average than females provided that the GPA is high enough.

iv. For a fixed value of IQ and GPA, females earn more on average than males provided that the GPA is high enough.

Answer: iv. For a fixed value of IQ and GPA, females earn more on average than males provided that the GPA is high enough.This statement is correct. Finding salary after graduation: Salary Total = Beta0 + Beta1 * X1 + Beta2 *X2 + Beta3 *X3 + Beta4 *X4 + Beta5 *X5 male = 50 + GPA∗20 + IQ∗0.07 + GPA∗IQ∗0.001 ((X3 = 0) female = 50 + GPA∗20 + IQ∗0.07 + GPA∗IQ∗0.001 + 35 + GPA∗(−10) (X3 = 1) female − male = 35 + GPA∗(−10) females earn more on average when GPA<3.5, males when GPA>3.5

(b) Wite down the least square function and then predict the salary of a female with IQ of 110 and a GPA of 4.0.

Least Squares Model regression is Salary = Beta0 + Beta1GPA + Beta2IQ + Beta3Gender + Beta4(GPA * IQ) + Beta5(GPA * Gender) + E

Given values IQ = 110, GPA = 4.0 Salary of female = 50 + (20 * 4.0) + (0.07 * 110) + (35*1) + (0.01 * 4.0 * 110) + ( -10 * 4 *1) = 50 + 80 + 7.7 + 35 + 0.0411 + (-40) = 132.74

(c) True or false: Since the coefficient for the GPA/IQ interaction term is very small, there is little evidence of an interaction effect. Justify your answer.

The statement is false. The magnitude of a coefficient alone does not determine statistical significance or evidence of an effect.What matters is whether the coefficient is significantly different from zero, usually assessed via a t-test or p-value. Even if the coefficient is small, it could still be statistically significant if the standard error is small.Conversely, a large coefficient could be insignificant if the variability is high.

Problem 8 - Extra Credit¶

Points: Max. 4

In this extra credit problem, you'll build a simple web scraper to collect and process text data. You'll write the code necessary to scrape lyrics for a desired artist. Your code should be structured such that one can easily execute your scraping functions for a given artist. There are three deliverables for this assignment:

  1. A set of functions necessary for scraping the lyrics of a specific artist.
  2. An example implementation of using your functions.
  3. A file of example output from your notebook implementation.

The specific approach that you take to structuring your code is up to you, but the final output .csv data should have the following columns (each row is a song from an artist that you choose):

  • Column 1: artist
  • Column 2: album
  • Column 3: song title
  • Column 4: URL of song lyrics
  • Column 5: song lyrics (all of the lyrics in one column)
  • Column 6: number of words in the song

Data Scraping: The actual scraping of data should be supported by separate functions that accomplish these tasks:

  1. Given an artist, identify all of their albums, songs, and links to songs.
  2. Given a set of song links (from step 1), collect the lyrics to each song and store them in a data frame.

In order to do this, you'll need to understand the structure of your lyrics site. The site you use is up to you, but all of this information should be available on lyrics.com.

Data Processing:

Once you've scraped the data, you'll need to do some simple text analysis to generate your columns of interest (feel free to do this as part of step 2 above, the collection of lyrics for each song or as a separate step entirely). Recall you are aiming to count the number of words in each song.

Example Implementation:

You should demonstrate the implementation of your data scraping functions with a particular artist. To do this you can simply set an artist, and run your scraping functions. The way in which you choose to structure your functions is up to you, as long as the implementation and documentation is clear. One way in which we'll test this is changing the artist to confirm the flexibility of your implementation.

It may look something like this:
